steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Uni-O4, an on-policy method that unifies offline and online deep reinforcement learning. Motivate the robot-learning pipeline, explain why offline-to-online fine-tuning is hard, position it against BPPO and prior work, and summarize our contributions and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivating scenario: robot policy trained online in simulator, offline on real data, online in real world
- Limits of online RL and offline RL
- Combining offline and online RL: why pre-train/fine-tune is hard in RL; prior fixes
- Trade-off between stability and optimality; value tracking in Figure 1(b)
- BPPO and its reliance on online evaluation
- Uni-O4: method
- Contributions and evaluation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivating scenario
  - RL robot must function and improve in real world
  - pipeline: online in simulator -> offline with real-world data -> online in real world
  - current RL algorithms focus on specific stages -> hard to train robots with a single unified framework
- Online vs offline RL
  - online RL: lots of interaction and exploration needed; prohibitive in many real-world applications
  - offline RL: learn from fixed dataset from other behavior policies; potential solution
  - but purely offline policy often not optimal: limited exploration, poor out-of-distribution (OOD) value estimation
- Combining offline and online RL
  - common paradigm: offline RL warm-starts policy and value function, then online RL stage boosts performance
  - pre-training/fine-tuning widely used in computer vision (cite), NLP (cite); direct use in RL non-trivial
  - offline RL needs regularization (conservatism (cite) or policy constraints (cite)) to avoid erroneous generalization to OOD data
  - used as initialization online -> fine-tuning instability from distribution shift
  - prior fixes during online stage: conservative learning, extra policy constraints (cite), Q-ensemble (cite), other value/policy regularization terms (cite)
  - still initial performance drop or asymptotical suboptimality (cite), from conservatism inherited from offline training
- Trade-off and Figure 1(b)
  - goal of offline-to-online RL: fine-tuning stability vs asymptotical optimality
  - challenges: inherent conservatism offline; off-policy evaluation difficulties in offline-to-online stage
  - track average V and Q values during fine-tuning, four methods
  - SAC (off-policy) and CQL (conservatism) fine-tune a CQL-trained offline policy; Off2on (cite) = Q ensemble-based fine-tuning
  - CQL: minimal Q improvement, over-conservatism -> suboptimal
  - Off2on and SAC: Q improves faster, but performance drops and unstable training early
  - Uni-O4: steady, rapid V improvement -> stable and efficient fine-tuning
- BPPO
  - Behavior Proximal Policy Optimization (BPPO) (cite): PPO (cite) objective with advantage replacement -> offline monotonic policy improvement
  - better offline performance than one-step offline algorithms (cite)
  - relies heavily on online evaluation to validate behavior policy improvement -> risks, extra costs
- Uni-O4
  - on-policy optimization unifying offline and online training, no extra regularization
  - motivated by BPPO: on-policy PPO objective for both offline and online RL, objectives aligned
  - offline policy evaluation (OPE) stage to evaluate updated policy -> multi-step policy improvement
  - OPE evaluation performance comparable to online evaluation methods
  - mismatch between offline dataset and estimated behavior policy: ensemble policies + policy diversity
  - better offline performance than BPPO, no online evaluation needed
  - then standard online PPO stage using pretrained policy and value function
  - seamless transit offline -> online; superior performance and efficiency in offline and offline-to-online
- Contributions and evaluation
  - Uni-O4: efficiency of on-policy RL in offline and offline-to-online learning
  - removes suboptimality and instability issues
  - unified design scales to online (simulator)-offline (real-world)-online (real-world); helps sim-to-real gap
  - evaluated on real-world legged robots and numerous D4RL (cite) tasks
  - simulated: beats SOTA offline and offline-to-online RL algorithms
  - real world: fine-tunes and adapts to challenging unseen environments with minimal interaction; beats SOTA sim2real and offline-to-online methods

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Imagine that a reinforcement learning robot needs to work and improve itself in the real world. The robot's policy might go through a pipeline where it is first trained online in a simulator, then offline with real-world data, and finally online in the real world. But current reinforcement learning algorithms usually focus on specific stages of learning, and this makes it harder to train robots with a single unified framework.

Online RL algorithms need a lot of interaction and exploration to get strong performance, and this is prohibitive in many real-world applications. Offline RL, where agents learn from a fixed dataset that was generated by other behavior policies, is a potential solution. However, a policy that is trained only with offline RL usually does not reach optimality, because of limited exploration or poor out-of-distribution (OOD) value estimation.

So a natural idea is to combine offline and online RL. The common paradigm here is to use an offline RL algorithm to warm-start the policy and the value function, and then have an online RL stage that further boosts the performance. Pre-training and fine-tuning is widely used in other machine learning domains like computer vision and natural language processing, but applying it directly to RL is non-trivial. The reasons are as follows. First, offline RL algorithms need regularization (called conservatism or policy constraints) so that they avoid erroneous generalization to OOD data. But when policies and value functions trained with these regularizations are used to initialize online learning, the distribution shift can make fine-tuning unstable. Previous works tried to deal with these challenges with conservative learning, by introducing additional policy constraints, Q -ensemble, or by adding other value or policy regularization terms during the online learning stage. However, these methods may still have an initial performance drop or asymptotical suboptimality in the online stage, because of the conservatism that is inherited from the offline RL training.

Offline-to-online RL algorithms aim to find a trade-off between stability of fine-tuning and asymptotical optimality. The challenges come from the conservatism that is inherent in the offline stage, and from the difficulties of off-policy evaluation in the offline-to-online stage. To make this clearer, we track the average values of the V and Q functions during fine-tuning with four different methods. In Figure 1(b), SAC (off-policy) and CQL (conservatism) are used to fine-tune the policy that was trained offline by CQL. Off2on is a fine-tuning method based on a Q ensemble. CQL improves the Q value only a little because of over-conservatism, and this leads to suboptimality. The Q value of Off2on and SAC improves faster, but both have performance drops and unstable training in the initial stage. Uni-O4 on the other hand shows steady and rapid improvement in the V values as fine-tuning progresses, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning that is both stable and efficient.

- BPPO
  - Behavior Proximal Policy Optimization (BPPO): PPO objective with advantage replacement -> offline monotonic policy improvement
  - better offline performance than one-step offline algorithms
  - relies heavily on online evaluation -> risks, extra costs
- Uni-O4
  - on-policy optimization unifying offline and online training, no extra regularization
  - motivated by BPPO: PPO objective in both phases, aligned
  - offline policy evaluation (OPE) -> multi-step policy improvement; comparable to online evaluation
  - ensemble policies + policy diversity for dataset / behavior policy mismatch
  - better offline than BPPO, no online evaluation
  - then standard online PPO stage with pretrained policy and value function; seamless transit
- Contributions and evaluation
  - efficiency of on-policy RL in offline and offline-to-online; no suboptimality / instability
  - scales to online (simulator)-offline (real-world)-online (real-world); sim-to-real gap
  - real-world legged robots + numerous D4RL tasks
  - beats SOTA offline and offline-to-online in simulation; beats SOTA sim2real and offline-to-online in real world with minimal interaction

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Imagine that a reinforcement learning robot needs to work and improve itself in the real world. The robot's policy might go through a pipeline where it is first trained online in a simulator, then offline with real-world data, and finally online in the real world. But current reinforcement learning algorithms usually focus on specific stages of learning, and this makes it harder to train robots with a single unified framework.

Online RL algorithms need a lot of interaction and exploration to get strong performance, and this is prohibitive in many real-world applications. Offline RL, where agents learn from a fixed dataset that was generated by other behavior policies, is a potential solution. However, a policy that is trained only with offline RL usually does not reach optimality, because of limited exploration or poor out-of-distribution (OOD) value estimation.

So a natural idea is to combine offline and online RL. The common paradigm here is to use an offline RL algorithm to warm-start the policy and the value function, and then have an online RL stage that further boosts the performance. Pre-training and fine-tuning is widely used in other machine learning domains like computer vision and natural language processing, but applying it directly to RL is non-trivial. The reasons are as follows. First, offline RL algorithms need regularization (called conservatism or policy constraints) so that they avoid erroneous generalization to OOD data. But when policies and value functions trained with these regularizations are used to initialize online learning, the distribution shift can make fine-tuning unstable. Previous works tried to deal with these challenges with conservative learning, by introducing additional policy constraints, Q -ensemble, or by adding other value or policy regularization terms during the online learning stage. However, these methods may still have an initial performance drop or asymptotical suboptimality in the online stage, because of the conservatism that is inherited from the offline RL training.

Offline-to-online RL algorithms aim to find a trade-off between stability of fine-tuning and asymptotical optimality. The challenges come from the conservatism that is inherent in the offline stage, and from the difficulties of off-policy evaluation in the offline-to-online stage. To make this clearer, we track the average values of the V and Q functions during fine-tuning with four different methods. In Figure 1(b), SAC (off-policy) and CQL (conservatism) are used to fine-tune the policy that was trained offline by CQL. Off2on is a fine-tuning method based on a Q ensemble. CQL improves the Q value only a little because of over-conservatism, and this leads to suboptimality. The Q value of Off2on and SAC improves faster, but both have performance drops and unstable training in the initial stage. Uni-O4 on the other hand shows steady and rapid improvement in the V values as fine-tuning progresses, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning that is both stable and efficient.

Recently, the work on Behavior Proximal Policy Optimization (BPPO) made significant advances by using the PPO objective with advantage replacement to get offline monotonic policy improvement. This gave better offline performance than one-step offline algorithms. However, BPPO relies heavily on online evaluation to check that the behavior policy has improved, and this brings risks and additional costs.

The core of this paper is an on-policy optimization method that unifies offline and online training without extra regularization, which we call Uni-O4. Motivated by BPPO, we use the on-policy PPO objective to optimize both offline and online RL, so the objectives in both phases are aligned seamlessly. Our approach uses an offline policy evaluation (OPE) stage to evaluate the updated policy and to get multi-step policy improvement. OPE has appealing evaluation performance, comparable to online evaluation methods. We also deal with the mismatch problem between the offline dataset and the estimated behavior policy by using ensemble policies and encouraging policy diversity. This way Uni-O4 improves the offline performance a lot compared to BPPO, and it does not need online evaluation.

After the offline optimization there is a standard online PPO learning stage which uses the pretrained policy and value function. With this algorithm, the transition between offline and online learning is seamless, and it gets superior performance and efficiency compared to current approaches in both offline and offline-to-online scenarios.

To summarize, our main contribution is Uni-O4, which shows that the on-policy RL algorithm is remarkably efficient in offline and offline-to-online learning. Uni-O4 gets rid of the suboptimality and instability issues in the current offline-to-online literature. Since the design is unified, it can be scaled up to more complex fine-tuning settings, like online (simulator)-offline (real-world)-and online (real-world), which helps with the sim-to-real gap in robot learning. We evaluate Uni-O4 on real-world legged robots and on numerous D4RL tasks. For the simulated tasks, the results show that Uni-O4 outperforms both SOTA offline and offline-to-online RL algorithms. Also, Uni-O4 does very well in real-world experiments, where it fine-tunes policies and adapts to challenging unseen environments with minimal interaction, and it surpasses SOTA sim2real and offline-to-online methods.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Imagine a scenario where a reinforcement learning robot needs to function and improve itself in the real world: the robot's policy might go through a pipeline of training online in a simulator, then offline with real-world data, and finally online in the real world. However, current reinforcement learning algorithms usually focus on specific stages of learning, which complicates the effort to train robots with a single unified framework.

Online RL algorithms require a substantial amount of interaction and exploration to attain strong performance, which is prohibitive in many real-world applications. Offline RL, in which agents learn from a fixed dataset generated by other behavior policies, is a potential solution. However, a policy trained purely by offline RL usually fails to reach optimality due to limited exploration or poor out-of-distribution (OOD) value estimation.

A natural idea is to combine offline and online RL, commonly by using an offline RL algorithm to warm-start the policy and the value function and then running an online RL stage to further boost performance. Although pre-training and fine-tuning is widely adopted in other machine learning domains such as computer vision [1] and natural language processing [2], its direct application to RL is non-trivial. First, offline RL algorithms require regularization (referred to as conservatism [3] or policy constraints [4]) to avoid erroneous generalization to OOD data. However, when policies and value functions trained with these regularizations are used to initialize online learning, distribution shift can lead to fine-tuning instability. Previous works have tried to address these challenges by employing conservative learning, introducing additional policy constraints [5,4,6,7], Q -ensemble [8,9], or incorporating other value or policy regularization terms [10,11,12] during the online learning stage. However, these methods may still suffer from an initial performance drop or asymptotical suboptimality [7,10,12] in the online stage, due to the conservatism inherited from offline RL training.

The objective of offline-to-online RL algorithms is to strike a trade-off between fine-tuning stability and asymptotical optimality. The challenges arise from the inherent conservatism of the offline stage and from the difficulties of off-policy evaluation during the offline-to-online stage. To illustrate this, we track the average values of the V and Q functions during fine-tuning with four different methods. As shown in Figure 1(b), SAC (off-policy) and CQL (conservatism) are used to fine-tune the policy trained offline by CQL, and Off2on [13] is a Q ensemble-based fine-tuning method. CQL shows minimal improvement in Q value due to over-conservatism, leading to suboptimality. The Q values of Off2on and SAC improve faster, but both suffer performance drops and unstable training during the initial stage. In contrast, Uni-O4 shows steady and rapid improvement in the V values as fine-tuning progresses, making it a favorable choice for stable and efficient fine-tuning.

Recently, Behavior Proximal Policy Optimization (BPPO) [14] made significant progress by adopting the PPO [15] objective with advantage replacement to achieve offline monotonic policy improvement, improving offline performance over one-step offline algorithms [16]. However, BPPO relies heavily on online evaluation to validate the improvement of the behavior policy, which introduces risks and additional costs.

At the heart of this paper is Uni-O4, an on-policy optimization method that unifies offline and online training without extra regularization. Motivated by BPPO, we employ the on-policy PPO objective to optimize both offline and online RL, seamlessly aligning the objectives of the two phases. Our approach uses an offline policy evaluation (OPE) stage to evaluate the updated policy and achieve multi-step policy improvement, and OPE shows appealing evaluation performance comparable to online evaluation methods. We further address the mismatch between the offline dataset and the estimated behavior policy by using ensemble policies and encouraging policy diversity. In this way, Uni-O4 significantly improves offline performance over BPPO without requiring online evaluation.

After offline optimization, a standard online PPO learning stage follows that leverages the pretrained policy and value function. The algorithm thus enables a seamless transition between offline and online learning while achieving superior performance and efficiency against current approaches in both offline and offline-to-online scenarios.

In summary, our main contribution is Uni-O4, which demonstrates the remarkable efficiency of the on-policy RL algorithm in offline and offline-to-online learning and gets rid of the suboptimality and instability issues in the current offline-to-online literature. Thanks to its unified design, it can be scaled up to more complex fine-tuning settings, such as online (simulator)-offline (real-world)-and online (real-world), which is useful for alleviating the sim-to-real gap in robot learning. We evaluate Uni-O4 on real-world legged robots and numerous D4RL [17] tasks. On simulated tasks, Uni-O4 outperforms both SOTA offline and offline-to-online RL algorithms. In real-world experiments, Uni-O4 also excels, fine-tuning policies and adapting to challenging unseen environments with minimal interaction and surpassing SOTA sim2real and offline-to-online methods.
